game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
With "Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You" Osmotic Studios and publisher Daedalic Entertainment deliver a narrative surveillance thriller that quietly turns its own core theme into self parody. The player is asked to watch over the privacy of others, while in the background a telemetry chain made of Steam, Unity and Mailchimp wakes up, of which not a single word can be found on the product page.

[h1]What does the product do?[/h1]On first launch the game already talks to Steam, fetches the SDR config for AppID 491950. In parallel Unity reaches out to Google Cloud, generates a persistent userid and ships a full hardware profile. Only after all of this does the player see a brief in game pointer to an external privacy notice.

[h1]Who operates the product?[/h1]Osmotic Studios GmbH (formerly Fellow Traveller)
Daedalic Entertainment GmbH (current publisher)

[h1]Which service providers are involved?[/h1]Osmotic Studios GmbH
Daedalic Entertainment GmbH
Valve Corporation
Unity Technologies
Google, LLC (infrastructure for Unity)
Intuit Mailchimp (owned by Intuit Inc.)
[noparse]Amazon.com, Inc.[/noparse]

[h1]What data is collected?[/h1]
Unique identifiers have been redacted for the review.
[b]Unity Analytics (no visible notice)[/b]
Unity 6000.3.8f1 fires POST requests to the Unity Analytics config and event endpoints. The endpoints resolve to Google Cloud in the United States.
[list][*] Persistent userid and deviceid, sessionid, session_count
[*] appid and build_guid
[*] Full hardware profile: CPU, RAM, VRAM, GPU vendor, driver, D3D12 feature level
[*] OS version, language, mainboard model, machine hostname
[*] Events appStart, appStop, SubsystemInfo, shaderRuntimeInfo
[/list]No OptIn is shown, tracking cannot be turned off inside the game.

[b]Steam Datagram Relay[/b]
The client fetches the Steam SDR configuration for the game and then opens 34 UDP connections to Frankfurt, Stockholm, London, Paris, Vienna, Warsaw, Amsterdam, New York, Chicago, Atlanta, Dallas, Los Angeles, Seattle, Sao Paulo, Buenos Aires, Santiago, Hong Kong, Tokyo, Seoul, Singapore, Mumbai, Sydney, Johannesburg and Dubai. For a pure single player thriller this fanout provides no benefit.

[b]Mailchimp newsletter[/b]
The in game newsletter sends first name, email and the tag "Orwell" straight to the Mailchimp REST API. The client uses a fixed HTTP Basic Auth credential baked into the build, "user:[redacted]-us14", which is a full Mailchimp API key visible in any network capture. The server response leaks list metadata, sender, statistics and a contact address (Papenstrasse 27, 22089 Hamburg) that differs from the one in the privacy notice. Headers reveal hosting in AWS us east 2.

[h1]GDPR violations in detail[/h1]
[b]Unity Analytics without consent[/b]
[list][*] Art. 5(1)a Transparency: Transmission starts before the user is informed
[*] Art. 6 Lawfulness: No consent, no documented legitimate interest
[*] Art. 7 Consent: No OptIn dialog, the pointer arrives too late
[*] Art. 13 Information obligation: Unity Analytics and Google Cloud are not named
[*] Art. 25 Privacy by Design: Tracking is default, no in game switch
[*] Art. 44ff Third country transfer: US Google Cloud, no SCC notice in game
[/list]
[b]Mailchimp newsletter[/b]
[list][*] Art. 5(1)f Integrity: The API key sits in plain text in the game binary
[*] Art. 13: Hosting in the US is not disclosed in game
[*] Art. 25: No server side email validation
[*] Art. 44ff: Third country transfer to the US, no visible safeguard
[/list]
[b]Steam SDR[/b]
Art. 5(1)c Data minimization: 34 worldwide relays for a solo title are excessive.

[h1]Privacy policy and Opt-in/Opt-out[/h1]
The Steam product page does not show or link any privacy policy or EULA. Inside the game a short pointer appears during profile creation, but only after Steam SDR and Unity have already shipped data abroad. The Steam age rating in Germany is "12 and up" while the Osmotic privacy notice itself requires a minimum age of 18. No age verification takes place.

A second oversight: the in game privacy notice is supposed to exist in English and German. In reality the "German" file is a word for word copy of the English text, only the headline reads "Datenschutzerklärung". A German speaking user has no proper localized notice available in game, which under Art. 12 GDPR is a serious flaw.

The notice itself does not name Unity Analytics, does not mention the Google Cloud infrastructure, does not list the Mailchimp pipeline and says nothing about a hardcoded API key inside the client.

[h1]Can this behavior be blocked?[/h1]
Yes, largely. The Unity Analytics endpoints, the Mailchimp REST API and the Steam SDR config request can all be blocked at the network layer without breaking gameplay. "Orwell" is a pure single player title, neither Unity Analytics nor SDR are required for it to run.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]"Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You" stages a surveillance state and trains the player to quietly oversee the data of strangers, while at the same time keeping a close eye inside its own engine room.

The Steam product page skips any data protection or EULA information, the in game pointer arrives too late and in a language version that is German only by name. Unity Analytics runs without a visible OptIn through Google Cloud in the United States, the newsletter pipeline goes through Mailchimp with an API key baked into the client, and Steam SDR opens 34 UDP connections worldwide for a solo title.

The thematic punch line lands twice here, once in the script and once in the network log.

[h1]Additional Info[/h1]
Additional details, including a full connection overview for blocking access, involved IPv4 addresses, company information and the German version of the review, are available as usual at [url=https://gameindustry.eu]GameIndustry[/url]. If you're interested, join the [url=https://steamcommunity.com/groups/penguindome]Penguin Domination[/url] group to stay informed about new reviews on Steam.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game is so-so; I want to recommend something *like* Orwell, but I'm on the fence about recommending Orwell itself. The game raises interesting issues, and the world would indeed be better off if everyone had at least the simulated experience of working with a large-scale surveillance system. I even usually found the story compelling, and I finished the game. However, the execution also felt a little disappointing.

The main gameplay problem, in my experience, was that sometimes I felt forced to take random or stupid-seeming actions just to see what it was that would finally advance the plot. This was in spite of the "handholding" cues the game uses to help you along.

Another thing that bothered me was a set of accuracy/realism concerns, which I will go on about below.

*************************************************

(Optional section about accuracy)

My main objection is that the game gives a poor sense of what doing an investigation with help of an Orwell-like system would actually be like in real life. In real life, either A) the computer would be a very powerful autonomous system and would make conclusions without human or involvement; or B) the human researcher would have sensible basic capabilities such as updating information, correcting machine-extracted snippets, and supplementing files with written analysis. The game tries to be somewhere in between, and in the process makes something that's unrealistic and sometimes annoying.  Also, there were also moments of "what the heck does the game want from me now", when I would add pointless or even incorrect information to the Orwell database solely to see if it would finally be the thing to move the plot forward.

The fact that you can't modify information in the Orwell crime database is pretty stupid on the face of things. To be fair, though, maybe it stands metaphorically for problems that could actually arise. For example, if two government agencies had a file on you, but the two were not in sync, the fact that you're not actually a criminal could be updated in one department's file without the second department learning about this, and perhaps the second database could lead to your extrajudicial killing.

The contextless, overaly literal way that information is passed from investigator to police is completely absurd. Perhaps this is a useful reflection of one possible way that an agency using an Orwell-type system could be dysfunctionally structured, though you'd hope that a bureaucracy wouldn't be quite that stupid. Or perhaps this limited information passing is symbolic of a potentially problem where two crime databases were linked, but could only communicate back and forth using a limited, contextless technical vocabulary, which would perpetuate misunderstanding. 

Perhaps the point of the game, though, is not to be right about the *particulars* of what could go wrong in a mass surveillance system, but more to give people an accessible experience that gives a general sense of creepiness.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I think I got this for free some months ago and now got to play it. It ran rather fine on an Ubuntu 18.04 lapttop with Nouveau drivers, game has native Linux support. 
You play as a worker for a surveillance program, sorting through the web and accessing peoples devices, looking for clues about terrorists. I cant really compare the game to anything, maybe it is similar to a graphical novel to some extent, as you have limited choices, but you do have to use your head, even if the game pretty much always at least tells you where to look for clues.  
It was almost an initimate experience to look into the character life, their private chats and calls. I feel like they could have added a bit more "useless" webpages, to make the game more authentic, but it is obvious that they tried  to give their characters depth, which is where the game shines. 
As the name of the game tells us, to some extent it is obviously a political/ethical game, even if done rather abstract (you work for "the nation", and pretty much everyone you investigate did something wrong). 
One thing I really appreciated, was that they show what can happen if systems like this make mistakes, which is something I feel like is not discussed enough as a counterargument to surveillance, besides the obvious ethical ones.  Overall the the game is an interesting experience, but not comparable to games like "Spec Ops -  The Line", where you really have to get your hands dirty, which lessens the impression of consequences of the players actions in my opinion.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
TL:DR, I myself enjoyed this game, great if you are into detective type work. Not a super exciting but overall 7/10

For the record, I got this while on sale for 5 dollars during steam sales. I see normally priced at 10 and that would be a maybe for buying it. 

So by the title you can guess that this has to do with big brother type surveillance, but in this you are acting as the investigator using the big brother program aka Orwell as a tool to piece together the story as it is happening about a alleged terrorist group. I can definitely see where someone could play this and find it dull and boring, but for me personally I found it intriguing and fun being able to access files and eavesdrop on conversation and collect intel from all sources. As well as building up character profiles and finding the relationships. One of few complaints I have is the moral dillema is kinda thrown in your face in the last moments of the game, which didn't ruin the game for me because it does then offer you a choice, but just felt very uninspired in a sense. The story leading to it was all around pretty good. While character development was great at times and very stereotypical in other times, the act of putting together character history and connections is actual quite fun. Especially in a sense where going through my first play through seemed to not matter and as though it seemed straight forward, looking at the achievements afterward and noticing I am missing half of them. And looking at the details of the achievements I can see where my actions can affect the story through the game. Similar to the character development, the story plot points were mostly good, but lack luster in other times. 

Gameplay itself feels immersive to me, but dont go into this expecting a whole bunch of mechanics or crazy things you can do. You are essentially sitting on a computer screen doing research and hacking into things. 

I will say, I went into this expecting there to be different cases as well, not to say I was dissapointed, I just thought there would be more to the game itself.

For 5 bucks and the first run through taking only 3 hours to complete I would recommend it, and I might go through again to see if I can knock out the other achievements and to really see what affect I have on the game.

review_text_raw:
ORWELL is a hybrid game somewhere between visual novel and point and click adventure. In the game, you are an investigator hired by the nation in testing out a new law which allows the government to spy on its citizens in order to find criminals. While this doesn’t sound too far off from where we are today, we can assume ordinary citizens aren’t having their wires tapped and all their online activity personally searched into. But that blurred line between what in this game is fiction and what is potential reality is where the game really shines, and pushes me to giving this game a general recommendation.
ORWELL starts off with investigating into a bomb that went off on a popular plaza and investigating a person of interest who was at the plaza. This is the only cutscene in the game and I really need to say that it shows how ugly the art style is. ORWELL has this odd polygonal art style that just doesn’t look right, and the game does nothing to utilize the style as well. Take a game like Wind Waker and the cell shading is important to the overall feel of the game, and the entire game would be very different if they had gone in a more realistic style. ORWELL does not earn that right to have an abstract art style, and it looks all the worse because of it. 
After the explosion, you begin digging into the meat of the game, which is going through people’s internet presence and phone calls and finding condemning information about them to fit them for the crime. The writing here then would be the important aspect to take away, and getting generally invested in the world or ORWELL should take precedence. However, this is another place where if the world of ORWELL was given to another developer with another vision, it probably would’ve been much more successful in world building that ORWELL currently is. The characters all generally fall into 2 categories; people who rebel against the government and people who are roped into rebelling against the government, and as such you get a lot of “it’s us or big brother vibes” when making your decisions which tends to not make the decisions feel organic. At several points in the game you can choose whether to report certain information to your supervisor and it affects how the supervisor views the target. However, these choices are often obviously superficial, and the contrasting information that you can give is usually contradicting in the sense that some information is outdated while other information is up to date. This is different than what an actual Orwellian inspired piece would aim for, where there are 2 facts that cannot exist within the same space and you are forced to accept both. For example, one contrasting information you need to choose between uploading to your supervisor is someone’s address. One is obviously right, and the other is outdated. It doesn’t mean the person didn’t use to previously live at the outdated address, but it’s just a matter of relevance. The game would be cooler if there were more instances of actual “doublethink” moments, instead of relying on portraying certain information in a correct or incorrect way. 
Speaking of being more Orwellian, the world of ORWELL is loaded with references to the novel by George Orwell, 1984. But this is another reason why the experience of the game is cheapened. A lot of the characters in the game are obvious references to people in 1984 and other dystopian media, such as a friend named Huxley or using the screenname w1n5t0n. If done sparingly, this could’ve been a neat little nod to the works of Orwell, but literally every character you interact with has some connection to the book, and the writing again suffers. It’s no longer a “hey, that’s a pretty neat reference,” but more so a “none of these characters seem original because the source material is being way overused.”
Ok, so all I’ve done is talk about the bad art style, the lacking writing, and non-significance of the gameplay, so why would I still recommend it? The reason I recommend it is because of that blurred line I mentioned at the beginning. That feel where you feel like you are gathering information about just another ordinary citizen, your mind begins to go what would this world really be like? If I send this review to my friends on messenger, what could someone get from my writing of it? One of the other things that happens a lot in the game is the people you talk to get implicated as well, so if I sent a message saying I was planning an attack to my group of friends, in ORWELL, everyone would be investigated on to find more evidence behind my potential crime and if they were involved in anyway. I think when some paths lead nowhere in ORWELL, it’s only a natural consequence that not everyone is going to be a criminal in the eyes of the government, but following the path to the end is pretty satisfying in the game. Despite the lackluster writing and world building, you do actually feel a voyeuristic guilt looking into everyone life between their social media accounts, medical records, college attendance, job records, blog posts, and so on. You can’t help but think if someone were to investigate me, they would find my screennames, my posts all over the internet, my video replays from streaming, and could trace words I said years ago to implicate me in something I was not a part of.
Altogether, the game has obvious flaws. It’s short, it has a forgettable art style, forgettable characters, and overall a forgettable plot. But playing through everything and seeing how everything plays out is thrilling in a way that no other game has ever provided for me. There is an ORWELL season 2 planned, and if they could just step away from the source material and feel more liberty to explore the world they’ve gone ahead and made, a lot of the issues I have with season 1 would be rectified. Overall, a 7/10. If you like dystopian media and the thought be being a voyeur into the lives of the ordinary citizens, give it a shot.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Game Summary: [/h1] 
This game doesn't fit into most normal game conventions and acts more like a cautionary tale.  By allowing the gamer to take the seat of a possible government agent in a program giving you so much power and access over people's lives, it lets you determine what you take away from it.  Is it a necessary evil for the government to have this much depth and access to what people are posting online, downloaded on their various devices, and talking about in their phone calls?  Or is that question alone already pushing too far, as people have an inherent right to privacy?  Wisely the game developer merely posits this to its audience, instead of preaching what is or isn't appropriate behavior in the 21st Century and beyond.  


[h1] Pros: [/h1] 
•	The first playthrough where I was intruding so far into people's lives made me feel uncomfortable.  Not scared or tense, just somewhat uncomfortable.  I think it's because invading people's privacy to this extent, knowing how easily the same thing could happen to you, is rather unsettling.  Medical records and mental health histories, various profiles and online communities you participate in (theoretically behind an alias), personal conversations and chats, all available for someone to read through.  For someone to comb through for any signs of instability, derangement, or evidence that this person isn't a law-abiding citizen, but a dirty crook.  This is dangerously close to criminalizing people for wrong-think.  
•	This game shines in its story and writing, because the characters feel real.  Their various profiles and conversations, how they become both paranoid and angry, but still only guessing at how bad things already are regarding the government's intrusion into their lives.  It gives the game a greater sense of reality and immersion, which is key.  They may not be rocket scientists, but they do take steps to avoid being screwed over, though if you're being a good big brother, it's already too late for them.  
•	I love that what I choose to upload can have a pretty big impact on how what the characters are saying and doing is interpreted.  It can either be seen as the acts of an innocent person, or the pattern of someone who's a low-down crook.  It raises the question of how any of us would look from the outside to someone who'd see all of our online activity.
•	The music acts as ambient background.  It's very low-key, and could theoretically be the sort of soft tune a government office would play to keep employees from getting too antsy.  This is for the most part, but when the climax of each day/act builds, then it picks up and gets you on edge.


[h1] Cons: [/h1] 
• 	Though it would take more time in both development and gameplay, it'd be nice if there were more people for you to look into who turned out to be red herrings.  It's not necessarily enjoyable being led astray, but it'd help sharpen the point of the game.  If you were being paranoid and looking at people through the lens of criminalizing everyone, you'd waste time and resources chasing false leads.  If you put on kids gloves and rationalized every viable threat as a misunderstanding, you'd let dangerous people slip on through.  What people say and mean aren't always the same, and one person's harmless rant is another's death threat.  
•	*Semi-Spoiler* I think one downside of the story is that all the key players are not inherently innocent.  They all have something significant to cover up, a reasonable way of implicating them for a crime and leading to their detention.  If they were merely guilty by association, and small phrases and statements were being pulled together to paint them as guilty, I think that would have had a stronger impact.  Otherwise, with how it is here, locking everybody up is justified.  You aren't throwing someone in jail who's wholly innocent.
•	Ironically, with how the last day plays out, you get so much material to look at, but are strictly limited on how much you can upload.  I get the idea of building tension this way, but I think it goes against what the game was going for.  The dilemma of the game wasn't in having to make a decision with so little information, but at digging for far too much, and falsely implicating innocent people on what you could piece together.  
•	Where the game suffers is through further playthroughs, as you see what happens if you try things a bit differently.  Since you're familiar with the characters, storyline, and reading their messages, it'd be nice if those could be sped up, instead of having to wait.  The chats are fairly crisp-paced considering they're supposed to be happening real-time, but it bogs down when you've seen it before.
•	Early in the game, video footage was used, and I thought that was going to come up again later.  I was quite disappointed that it only had a place in the game once, and I do feel misled that everything you analyze in the game is just text, whether a call, chat, or profile.
•	It'd be nice if some of the items which are definitively pointless and not useful anymore would be cleared away.  For instance, all the random news clips and headlines, since most of them had no pertinence to the exploration for more information.  
•	Sometimes I had a really hard time dragging points of interest into profiles or disabling them.  The controls were a bit floaty and annoying to work with.


[h1] Conclusion: [/h1] 
Whether we like it or not, whatever we post online is going to exist indefinitely.  Since so much information is out there, it does raise the issue of who would be keeping track of these matters, who might be lurking without our knowledge to try and keep tabs over us.  Whether it's the government or not, people can do some pretty sketchy things with computers, and this knowledge and power is a great temptation, tool, and force.  This game acts as a simulation for what can be done with that kind of power.  A bumbling buffoon who doesn't take it seriously, could allow guilty parties to slip out of facing justice.  An overly authoritarian and distrustful person could throw people behind bars for any minor infraction.  True, laws may have been broken, but should we throw away privacy and autonomy to catch such small fries?  We'd be foolish to hand over such power carelessly, as it could be so easily abused, but total restriction could also prevent heinous monsters from being caught and prosecuted.  These are hefty matters worthy of being discussed in the public sphere, and this game highlights both sides of that discussion.  If you're looking for a game in a conventional sense, you'd be disappointed, but if you're open to an experience with an important message at its core, Orwell has a lot to offer.  

Be careful if you write a reply or comment on this review.  You don't know who could be reading it.  It's alright if you don't necessarily agree with everything the government does, but don't be overly critical and certainly don't call for a revolution or anything CRAZY like that.  We'd HATE for there to be a group trying to overthrow the government, right?  Oh crap, I hear them at my door.  They're on to me!  Fight while you still can, don't be compliant, resist, fight on, fi-!  *Device has been disconnected*

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Excellent game.

To those who know the references and like the source material this game is based off of, this is perhaps the best Big Brother/Orwellian Surveillance system simulator I've seen so far, and is well worth the price its asking for. 

Fans of Papers, Please will probably enjoy this game just as much. Except instead of being the Border Crossing Guard, think of yourself as the Investigator for their Surveillance Corps.

Its a short game, sure, you can beat it once probably within 4 hours, but it does have some replayability (plus the fact that there is no hard save points, the game constantly saves after everything you do with no way of going back outside of making a new profile, so it forces you to choose wisely). To me, the shortness is forgiveable for how much this game costs (which isn't much).

The writing is amazing for it being a game with only written dialogue, the characters feel real and individual and you're the spider trying to weave out the web of how they fit into the plot that's going on. It also does a great job of getting you into the role of being an Investigator of a secret service public spying agency, you feel as if you're in the game just as much as any of them at times.

The art style is consistent and works for the game that this is, but IMO they could have had clear photos and models and you would have had the same game, this style merely gives it a more individual feel rather than it being like any other game like this.

The gameplay is simple, but great if you're into investigative puzzle-solving.

The music is very good for eliciting responses and making you feel certain emotions at particular times, as its supposed to, though IMO it moves a little too fast at times in transitions. You're often left with an abrupt music cue and wondering "What the hell, what did I just find?" before you can properly read what found. But otherwise its good.

Only encountered one bug at the very end of the game where it froze and looped the last second or two of the music track I was listening to, and I had to exit out with alt-tab, but I had beaten the playthrough by that point so it wasn't a huge deal.

All and all, a great game for the price its asking for, and if you're a fan of the type of genre this is.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The premise is interesting, the UI is fantastic, but...

The writing doesn't work. Not to me, at least.

So the idea is, you're an anonymous member of the public working with a new program that's half google, half snooping software. You're assigned a case - the first one is about a bomb placed in a plaza, and thanks to surveillance cameras you're assigned to look up everything about a suspect. So far so good, right? There's the relevant question of whether it's right to spy on someone in the name of public safety, there's a mystery to solve...

But it falls apart. Your supervisor is all "she has a police record, let's snoop on her" and okay, good enough reason to investigate...her faux-facebook page, her faux-portfolio, news websites, etcetera. Except that none of these websites feel like they were ever used by real people, her facebook timeline feels bizarre, like she's a fascimile of a human being, and when you get to eavesdrop on her text messages with her boyfriend, again it feels false?

Everything is off, and not in a good way. And your supervisor is so ready to pin the entire case on her because she's joined an activist group that organizes protests against the surveillance state.

It's too on the nose, with writing that doesn't sell to me that I'm snooping on real people, with a wonky "this is taking place in real time" - but it's not, really, you only get to eavesdrop on people's text conversations when you unlock them, not when they happen - and it all just feels clumsy.

In a game that's only got its writing going for it, having a fantastically slick UI isn't going to keep me playing it. Which is a bummer! The questions this game is asking are relevant, and it's so slick and pretty to look at I want to dig into it! ... But sadly it's just not compelling.

Bummer.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game will have you be FBI in a world where the NSA collects and store [i]everything[/i] but doesn't share it with you.

First off I rarely do reviews here on Steam but this game deserves it. Not because it's inherently bad game design, I don't think it is so much. Not because I just personally didn't like it or anything like that. I actually enjoyed the design choices both in terms of gameplay and aesthetics, it just works as is, nothing great but nothing terrible either. game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What a wasted opportunity.

I went into this game wanting to like it - I really did. To be clear - I played through the entire game, finishing each of the 5 chapters.

Orwell is ostensibly a game about a surveillance state gone terribly wrong - but almost at every opportunity, it fails to make any meaningful point and constantly gets in its own way.

It starts bad. Rather than giving you, as a player, the agency to incriminate and potentially ruin the lives of the people you are surveilling, the game immediately puts you at arms-length. You are nothing more than a data collector with the ability to find and store information, but not make any meaningful analysis or conclusions about this data. Worse, it pairs you with the clumsily-written and drearily heavy-handed Symes - the *actual* investigator, who acts on the information you upload and is a constant source of awkward, immersion-breaking, and stupid commentary. 

It's true that, in principle, the data you choose to upload can affect the lives and outcomes of the people whose privacy you're invading - the trouble is that there's no real incentive to do so. Oftentimes, you must upload certain pieces of data in order to move the story along - which makes sense, because you're nothing more than a glorified data monkey clicking blue text and throwing it into a database. If you choose to hide a piece of information, it's not clear whether or not you'll be able to progress through the story. If you get something wrong (in the extremely limited range of things you are even allowed to get wrong), there are few consequences - an issue exacerbated by how distanced you are from everything that goes down. You don't really get to make the call, figure out the deduction, or even choose whether or not you should be wielding the awesome power you do. You either progress the story, or you don't - Symes is the one who gets to actually decide.

What's worse is that each of the characters in the game are utterly unlikable - the crimes you investigate them for are legitimate crimes that hurt real innocents and pose genuine dangers to the society in which they inhabit - the moral quandary that this game should so naturally lend itself to (the invasion of privacy, the loss of intimacy, that everybody is a criminal under mass surveillance, etc.,) is utterly and absolutely wasted. Instead, you are railroaded through a specific set of documents, webpages, and chats (not giving you any opportunity to actually deduce anything) in which not one of the horribly written characters manages to endear themselves.

Ultimately, this game is trying to tell you two stories - a by the numbers B-grade mystery plot filled with unlikable and annoying characters, and a study of the evolution of mass surveillance in an increasingly tech-focussed society. In so doing, they tell neither one well. They did an incredible disservice to a barely-interesting character study of modern revolutionaries, and an even greater disservice to the core (and seemingly obvious!) issues with state-driven, indiscriminate surveillance.

Let's not even start with the UI. What begins as a somewhat interesting ability to listen in on conversations quickly becomes a tiresome and arduous chore - there are a couple of moments in which listening in on a conversation live makes sense, but these moments are few and far between. For the most part, you are treated to a disastrously slow chat message filled with stilted dialogue and unfortunate Fellow Kids idioms, or an equally slow voice transcription. I quickly began to dread these moments, rather than feel the rush of uncovering a potential clue.

At no point do you feel like a data wizard, an unscrupulous detective, or even a curious and detached researcher. You just feel bored. 

Orwell is, despite its polished presentation, a total and undeniable bust. 

Desperately trying to cram all of the social commentary it should have been exploring over the entire game into its final chapter, it fails to make a meaningful statement about mass surveillance and the police state. 

Having written shallow, stupid, stereotypical characters with zero likable traits or humanizing aspects (each of whom are also genuine suspects in an act of actual terrorism) it fails to present a compelling character study of the 21st-century revolutionary.

By railroading you during every part of the core gameplay loop and anchoring you at the waist with a bumbling, intrusive character (who gets to make *all* the calls and draw all the *actual* conclusions), they fail to provide a satisfying, thrilling, or even baseline interesting detective experience.

Finally, by forgetting the most fundamental principles in their clunky, limited, and careless design, they failed to provide an even halfway tolerable interface. 

I didn't even get to enjoy interacting with the game.

Orwell is a disaster. You will get nothing from it, no insight, no emotion, no deductions, and no surprises. It wastes every bit of the opportunity it had to say something meaningful.

This is my Two Minutes Hate - and Orwell deserves every second of it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The game advertises itself as a Big Brother simulator, but it doesn't [i]quite[/i] reach that level of depth and intrigue that kind of premise could reach.

However, I don't think Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You isn't a bad game at all. I think it's definitely a concept that is executed well. You play as an investigator who's collecting information on a variety of people through public channels, such as social media outlets, and private channels such as one's email. These pieces of information are used as evidence to solve the crime you're assigned to.

There is some decision-making in the game and it was interesting to see how the conversation changes between characters after performing certain actions. There are a couple of routes to take, but ultimately, the resolution is relatively the same. I don't mind this that much, and I honestly think true choice games are difficult to make, unless you have the resources as a studio.

However, the main element I found to be lacking was the story; it was rather light. There are a few tense moments in the story, but overall, it seemed like the writers decided on a safer route. I was expecting somewhat darker and more philosophical themes to be used in the game. They are touched upon lightly, but not expanded to play any significant role. Given the premise, there's a whole world of deep possibilities that could be played out, but the writing just scratches the surface of this. In the end, I found myself wanting a little more out of the game.

All in all, the game was less than satisfactory for me and I'd give it a neutral rating, if I could. If you're new to the whole 'mass surveillance' idea and want to see a taste of what a game could do with that idea, then sure, go play this. But if you want something deeper, this isn't quite it.

Side note: I also bought and played the DLC and it's just more of the same, in my opinion.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Creepy and well-written, Orwell tells the tale of what happens when the state gets unfettered access to your communication data, whether that be from the telephone or the internet. It's very topical, but it should be added that the scope of the access you have makes the recent "Snooper's Charter" in the UK look like lightweight. Nevertheless, your ability to screw with people's lives really hits home, especially when the twist at the end is revealed and all the consequences of your actions - and how misinterpreted data can be overblown - is laid bare.


That said, the game stays rather neutral in its moralising. It's clear the developers are anti-surveillance, as those *for* it would find the moral ambiguity of this game inconvenient, but they are not trying to whack you over the head with ideology. If you decide to come to the conclusion that, despite being messy at times, surveillance is a necessary evil then this game allows you to come to that conclusion. But it's going to push the extremes of what all-encompassing surveillance can do before it lets you come to that conclusion.

And while the politics of this game are clearly unavoidable, Orwell is also a pretty neat detective story, if not very typical. Instead of being in the front line looking for evidence, your sleuthing is invisible, but otherwise it has all the hallmarks of a good whodunnit, including red herrings, characters with strong motivations, and a twist at the end.

I'm not sure what else to say, really. It's pretty good and I happily recommend it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is engrossing and more than a bit disturbing considering the implications of some very real things that are happening in the world right now. More of an interactive novel than a proper game, it nonetheless pulled me in for the 3-4 hours it took to reach the end of it, as well as a couple of replays to try out different paths.

It's not perfect, though; there's no challenge in actually getting the information you require since it's highlighted for you and you simply have to upload it, which sort of takes most of the initiative out of your hands. You do get to decide how certain characters are viewed based on how much you pass on to the powers that be, and your choices affect how they're treated and what happens to them, but the prevailing narrative is more or less canned, on-rails, and you can't do very much to affect how it plays out other than within a narrow scope. Some of the decisions you make do have very profound consequences for the individuals concerned, and the first time through I did have a few things I deeply regretted because of what happened as a result.


The biggest downside is that the game is short and fairly linear; there are only so many branches/possibilties to explore, so once you've exhausted them, there's really not much replay value. 

I've seen a few comparisons made to Papers, Please, which is less slick to play but rather more profound to actually experience because of the huge number of variations in how it can go. Orwell comparatively lacks depth, but because you spend more time with all the characters and get to know them better (since you're snooping through their gadgets and availing yourself of some very personal details of their lives), what happens to them matters a lot more to you. At least, it mattered more to me. In Papers Please I was more concerned with getting myself and my family out of dodge. 

Think of Orwell as an interactive dystopian techno-thriller and you've got a pretty good idea what you're in for.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] How far are you willing to go to protect the populace? [/h1]

[i]Orwell[/i] is a “visual novel” style game in which you have the ability to follow cyber-breadcrumbs in order to slowly uncover suspect’s online lives. Your goal? Stop a terrorist organization (?) from bombing public spaces. Your tools? As an agent, you are privy to the entirety of your target’s posts, articles, phone calls, emails, etc. Use this information to reveal more and more relevant webpages and conversations. The catch? You’re overlooked by a supervisor and you must choose what information to upload. This supervisor can only see the bits of information you feed him, so choose wisely or risk ruining an innocent’s life. The challenge? Upload only enough information to gain new leads, but not jump to conclusions. 

Are you really helping the greater good by invading the privacy of the few? Or have you caused more harm than good, muddling in affairs you should have never been in? Are the internet spies of today, really the superheroes of tomorrow? Find out by stepping into these large, cyber shoes. Act quickly and stop a harmful event in its tracks, or wait it out and discover it was a false alarm. Big brother is watching you. You are watching the people. Lives are on the line. Decide. 

Then watch as you say, [b]“I never meant for this to happen.”[/b]

Let me start off this review by saying I’m one who really enjoys a story-based game. I particularly enjoy consequence based story games (like [i]Telltale[/i]). If that’s not your cup of tea, this game is not for you. If you’re still interested, here’s the pros and cons for the game so far.

[h1]Pros:[/h1] [b]Interesting social commentary.[/b] There’s no denying that this is the age of technology, and with that comes a whole new slew of problems that our forefathers never could have foresaw when drafting the constitution. [i]Orwell[/i] heavily and obviously alludes to the current hot topics of freedom of internet access, government access to our personal files and correspondences, and general cyber security we see crop up in the news time and time again. 

[b]Easy interface.[/b] There’s not much to learn but drag and drop. Your un-uploaded data chunks are marked so you don’t lose track of what you’ve read, need to read, and are saving for later.

[b]More unique game flow.[/b] Events don’t happen unless you upload data chucks, leaving you to explore the branches of plot in whatever order feels natural to you. It does still feel a bit restricted, though, (see “A bit linear, limited” in cons) a perhaps more of a pseudo-free-directional choice. (But isn’t the concept of freedom what this game is all about?) 

[b]Intriguing artwork.[/b] The geometric artistic style lends itself to unconsciously nod its head towards the cyber-oriented world of the game. It ties in beautifully to the theme of the game—from the logo to the interface—without being too aggressive.

[h1]Cons:[/h1] [strike][b]A better save system!![/b][/strike] Update has added a rewind system, but I have not played since [strike]I cannot stress this enough. Since this is a consequence-based game, I’d like to be able to start from the end episode one, or so, with my decisions staying the same, and only make changes to my decisions from there out, with my profiles branching out from my first play through plot line. Starting over from the beginning is too much of a grind. Even a way to speed up messaging/call text on the second (and beyond) playthrough would be better for acheivement hunters or people just curious about the other endings. Examples of games with a good save system for this style of gameplay include [i]A Wolf Among Us[/i] and [i]Papers, Please.[/i][/strike]

[b]A bit linear, limited.[/b] There were some moments I wish some bit of text was highlighted (you may only drag and upload highlighted data chunks) since I wanted to explore that avenue of inquiry, but [i]Orwell[/i] had other plans. This gave the game a restricted feeling. It does not leave the game open to a world of naturally-occurring red herrings (only game-constructed ones, not user constructed), which I think would have added much more depth to the game. Also, it’s glaringly obvious which pieces of text carry great significance. (Those will be the ones with conflicting evidence) so sometimes the challenge of deciding to report information right away or wait was quite discernible, offering no challenge. Although, I will say that there are a few nuggets of data I uploaded without believing they would have as large of a consequence as they did. 

[b]Short.[/b] There’s only a little over forty minutes of game play per episode, and with five episodes, this leads to roughly four hours of gameplay (assuming you don’t replay events). I follow a rule of thumb of at least $1 to 1 hour of gameplay, so in that regard, it’s a bit pricey. Just wait for a sale. 

[h1]Remark:[/h1] [b]Play in one sitting[/b] (or as close to that as possible, if you don't have a full 4-5 hours to dedicate to one game) The flow and length of the game lends itself to be optimally played in one sitting. Taking a break and not have a comprehensive refresher (like the cinematic playbacks of key choices in [i]Telltale[/i] games) of your choices and actions is jarring to the enjoyment of the storyline in my opinion.

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
[b]I’d recommend buying [i]Orwell[/i] when on sale.[/b] It has an interesting and captivating storyline, despite some need of polishing. The interface, flow, and artwork lend itself to be an immersive experience into the lives of the people you are spying on to protect. Also, the current social commentary gives a real-world depth to the game. It does feel a bit restricting at times, and the story is short. The save system leaves much to be desired, since I would like to more easily explore all possibilities of my choices. But, despite these factors it was still enjoyable and fun to play.

Then watch as you say, [b]“I never meant for this to happen.”[/b] Let me start off this review by saying I’m one who really enjoys a story-based game. I particularly enjoy consequence based story games (like [i]Telltale[/i]). If that’s not your cup of tea, this game is not for you. If you’re still interested, here’s the pros and cons for the game so far. [h1]Pros:[/h1] [b]Interesting social commentary.[/b] There’s no denying that this is the age of technology, and with that comes a whole new slew of problems that our forefathers never could have foresaw when drafting the constitution. [i]Orwell[/i] heavily and obviously alludes to the current hot topics of freedom of internet access, government access to our personal files and correspondences, and general cyber security we see crop up in the news time and time again. [b]Easy interface.[/b] There’s not much to learn but drag and drop. Your un-uploaded data chunks are marked so you don’t lose track of what you’ve read, need to read, and are saving for later. [b]More unique game flow.[/b] Events don’t happen unless you upload data chucks, leaving you to explore the branches of plot in whatever order feels natural to you. It does still feel a bit restricted, though, (see “A bit linear, limited” in cons) a perhaps more of a pseudo-free-directional choice. (But isn’t the concept of freedom what this game is all about?) [b]Intriguing artwork.[/b] The geometric artistic style lends itself to unconsciously nod its head towards the cyber-oriented world of the game. It ties in beautifully to the theme of the game—from the logo to the interface—without being too aggressive. [h1]Cons:[/h1] [strike][b]A better save system!![/b][/strike] Update has added a rewind system, but I have not played since [strike]I cannot stress this enough. Since this is a consequence-based game, I’d like to be able to start from the end episode one, or so, with my decisions staying the same, and only make changes to my decisions from there out, with my profiles branching out from my first play through plot line. Starting over from the beginning is too much of a grind. Even a way to speed up messaging/call text on the second (and beyond) playthrough would be better for acheivement hunters or people just curious about the other endings. Examples of games with a good save system for this style of gameplay include [i]A Wolf Among Us[/i] and [i]Papers, Please.[/i][/strike] [b]A bit linear, limited.[/b] There were some moments I wish some bit of text was highlighted (you may only drag and upload highlighted data chunks) since I wanted to explore that avenue of inquiry, but [i]Orwell[/i] had other plans. This gave the game a restricted feeling. It does not leave the game open to a world of naturally-occurring red herrings (only game-constructed ones, not user constructed), which I think would have added much more depth to the game. Also, it’s glaringly obvious which pieces of text carry great significance. (Those will be the ones with conflicting evidence) so sometimes the challenge of deciding to report information right away or wait was quite discernible, offering no challenge. Although, I will say that there are a few nuggets of data I uploaded without believing they would have as large of a consequence as they did. [b]Short.[/b] There’s only a little over forty minutes of game play per episode, and with five episodes, this leads to roughly four hours of gameplay (assuming you don’t replay events). I follow a rule of thumb of at least $1 to 1 hour of gameplay, so in that regard, it’s a bit pricey. Just wait for a sale. [h1]Remark:[/h1] [b]Play in one sitting[/b] (or as close to that as possible, if you don't have a full 4-5 hours to dedicate to one game) The flow and length of the game lends itself to be optimally played in one sitting. Taking a break and not have a comprehensive refresher (like the cinematic playbacks of key choices in [i]Telltale[/i] games) of your choices and actions is jarring to the enjoyment of the storyline in my opinion. [h1]Conclusion:[/h1] [b]I’d recommend buying [i]Orwell[/i] when on sale.[/b] It has an interesting and captivating storyline, despite some need of polishing. The interface, flow, and artwork lend itself to be an immersive experience into the lives of the people you are spying on to protect. Also, the current social commentary gives a real-world depth to the game. It does feel a bit restricting at times, and the story is short. The save system leaves much to be desired, since I would like to more easily explore all possibilities of my choices. But, despite these factors it was still enjoyable and fun to play.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A wonderful game.

Have you played a Telltale game recently? Do you notice that most of your decisions are cosmetic or mere distractions except for the one or two major decisions? You probably have thought about that. There are a number of different reactions to this fact. Either the games are so interesting you just don't notice/care (Walking Dead), you're willing to let it slide (The Wolf Among Us), or it absolutely spoils the game by making the player feel powerless (Game of Thrones).

What if there could be a game that took into account every decision the player made and changed the plot accordingly?

Orwell does this. In a way that is sometimes overwhelming.

The premise of the game is somewhat reminiscent of Papers, Please. You are hired as a government worker. Your job is to be connected to a massive spy-network which has access to the entire internet and can bypass all privacy settings. You're tasked with investigating a terrorist incident, finding suspects, and hopefully stopping their plans before they happen.

You cannot directly decide what or who to investigate. What you do is you highlight certain passages you uncover (from people's blogs, text messages, phone conversations, etc) and submit them to the system, which will then build its case in the direction the evidence will go. One of the first conflicts you're given to resolve is the investigation of a young woman who is a political activist. One who writes on her political essays "We are dedicated to peaceful means to promote political change," and then writes on her personal blog in a fit of anger: "DEATH TO ALL WHO DISAGREE WITH US!"

Do you submit the intellectual and rational example in an attempt to give the subject the benefit of the doubt, or do you decide the words spoken emotionally are her true feelings?

If you're getting the impression the game is meant to be a parable about the futility of massive surveilance and how invasive it is, there's one problem with that assessment: it's possible to actually succeed and prevent crimes this way.

The game gives the player a lot of credit in this respect. They don't settle for a straightforward storyline with a didactic message. There are certainly messages conveyed about surveillance and its implementation, how it affects people, etc., but the game's storyline is genuinely about the characters and the environment they're in, not a tract about politics.

If the gameplay sounds boring, be assured in that the game actually manages to make many scenes genuinely tense and thrilling as well. You will scramble to acquire more datachunks before time runs out and genuinely panic at some points.

It's a truly great experience, well worth the price, and I heartily recommend it because it really does make it feel like every choice you make, every little bit of data you feed to this huge system that guides the investigation really does matter.

Though there is one low point which I'll discuss. It involves some spoilers, so stop reading if you want to avoid them.


***spoilers***


The most conflicting thing about this game is its ending. Specifically there are three different types of endings with some variations between them. In this it's again similar to Papers, Please because the endings are either "Stay loyal to the government," "betray the government," or "do something else."

The problem is that none of these endings really... 'satisfy'.

With Papers, Please, all the endings were satisfying. If you stayed loyal to the government, you were congratulated for being a loyal citizen. You were able to keep your job. You were assured your life would continue and it would be good for your character. This is a very satisfying ending.

If you betrayed the government, you were also congratulated for doing so. You were given a vision of a new, better society you were helping to build and that you had genuinely done the right thing in helping the revolution. This is *also* a very satisfying ending. They both manage to be positive, even when the player does the exact opposite things. Perhaps it's not entirely rational, but a player who goes either path will enjoy their ending.

In Orwell though... none of the endings feel completely positive.

If you stay loyal to the government, if you prove the surveillance can work and bring down the terrorists and get the "ultra-loyal" ending, it leaves a bad taste in your mouth because you still don't feel like justice was done.

If you completely disobey the government, that doesn't feel right either. It doesn't feel like the people in opposing the government are right, or even doing things out of 'necessity'.

When I complete a video game, I want to feel some accomplishment. I'm fine with middling 'you did some bad things and good things, so you get a middling ending where both bad and good things happen,' but if I really put the time and effort to try to do everything 100% right by people, I want to feel congratulated with a positive feel-good "You did a good thing" ending. I want the game to acknowledge I tried. In that case, I didn't feel like there was enough celebration, so to speak. There's no 'ultra-happy ending'. Not necessarily a non-confrontational ending where no one is hurt, but at least one in which the guilty are punished and the innocent are spared.

The options that are presented for you to choose for your 'ending' are valid choices that I liked, but I think it could've used just a little bit more development to make it feel like a 'reward'. That is my only criticism, but even then, I replayed it through to see all the different variations, so it's not a game-ruiner by any means.

Again, it's recommended if you like story-oriented games with unique gameplay ideas.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This seemed like a novel and interesting title when I first found it. After playing through I can say this is so much more.

When you talk about games that move you people might say things like Mass Effect, Deus Ex, and various other story based games, or if we look at the indie side of thing you will get: Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons, This War of Mine, and To the Moon.

I can tell you this game does it just as effectively, if not more so, because YOU -- the actual you sitting at your computer -- are a charter in the game. Add that to the decisions you have to make and the pressures you will feel -- even though it's just  a game -- it will make you react to the story almost as though it is real.

You will care about what is happening, deeply.

You will be unable to stop, just like with a good book.

And all that's just the story, this game is also basically a case study of a surveillance state, like in the book 1984 (as you might have guessed from the title of the game) and references to the book are goddamn everywhere.

So, should you buy it? IMO yes you should it is an amazing experience.
If you like visual novels (Ace Attorney comes to mind) you will love this. (as it basicly is one)
If you like a good book you will love this.
If you like just a good story you will love this

And for that reason, should you consider ever buying this, I vehemently urge you to go in completely blind -- if you haven't read the description about this game on steam, don't. This game is better the less you know of  what is going on when you start, and if you spoil it all the magic will be lost.

However should you come here expecting a good "GAMING" experience and you care little for the story you will be very disappointed with this game as gameplay is as simple if not more than many of the classic flash games on sites like addictinggames.

I give it a 9/10 though it pains me to do so

I just can't give it a perfect to to some niggles in the interface that are simply annoying.

Regardless you should play this game (try the demo, it's part of the actual game not some curated bull crap like ubisoft does)

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Intresting premise,  poor execution. In the attempt to create stakes for the players decision, Orwell goes out of it's way to obfuscate or even fail to present clarfying information until after the decision is made. It also prevents refinement of past data with new context. Being forced to compete in the 20 meter jump to conclusions in order to find the context you needed to make that conclusion is beyond obxnoxious. This is made worse by there being minimal clarity to what the data you've supplied will be intreperted as, and that intreptation is final with little abitliy to recontextualize. 

This of course undermines any moral arguement the game attempts to present or have you consider. Over surveillance, the effect of technology on the governments ability to monitor it's citizens and so forth are good topics to explore. However demonstarting the conquences by forcing the player to pick up the idiot ball does no one any favours.  

The concept is good, if you can deal with being forced to make uncontextualized leaps of judgement you might enjoy the game. But the inability to use good inquirial practices like preserving and rexamining conflicting data in light of new evidence kills the game for me.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I've only played one case. Maybe it gets better but I already hate it. This is a game that saw [i]Papers Please[/i] and a Telltale game and thought: these should be one thing. They shouldn't. It wants to have the humanism of a game that is mostly just a postmodern exploration of character ([i]Her Story, Analogue: A Hate Story[/i]), but it also wants you to make binary data choices on which set of data to pass on to your superior without being given enough information to know how it will be interpreted.

[i]Papers Please[/i] presents very clear outcomes for the majority of your choices and the moral weight they have and gives a context for why a choice must be made anyway.  By presenting the status quo of a job which you must do for a family who could starve, the game allows for depth of story, a context for why things must be as they are and real stakes for the choices that are made.

Telltale games often don't pre-empt the outcomes of your choices, but often these choices are superfluous because what matters is the character drama. But the thing is that the games sensationalize these choices and make them feel like they could matter, even when they don't. This character could die instead of this one, you might find out a different set of information, but the structure of the story and the characters' movement through it remains intact. 

When you mash them up what you get is a completely unnuanced yes-no/good-bad moral choice system ala Fable in a world that resembles the real one too closely for that to not be cringe-worthy. Only the binary isn't good/bad because as someone who is already spying on someone and potentially ruining their life just to test if you can get access to the next document by adding chunks that seem only tangentially related but will be interpreted as reason to call the police, you're always bad. And if that's what the game's political critique boils down to, then I got it. Thumbs up.

"Are they really terrorists?" the game's description asks. And the answer is no. I could have guessed that from the bugged out clip following her getting on a bus that only played the second time I started a new game because the first one I hit a dead end and had no choice but to just start adding data at random hoping something would trigger only to have to google and find out it was a known bug and I just had to restart from the start. So thanks, I hate it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
ORWELL - 3/10

Quick Review:  A slightly more interactive version of a visual novel, Orwell tries to claim some of the success legendary books like 1984 and Brave New World have. Unfortunately it's cliche and boring characters, simple and tedious gameplay, long wait times and confusing target audience make this a game I can't possibly recommend.

Story
-------
You play as an investigator who is hired from outside a country where a new system called "Orwell" is put in place. In it's early stages, Orwell is being used to collect data and spy on people in order to keep the public safe. After a bomb goes off in Freedom Plaza, your job is to find who is behind the bombing by investigating someone who has a small criminal history that was at the scene and see what you can discover from there.

The story isn't particularly interesting and while there are some major plot events I don't think they hit their intended mark for me because I wasn't particularly captivated in the first place. The characters you have to investigate are all the typical "fuck the government" protesters with little to no original personality traits. Everything is unoriginal and cliche as can be.

Gameplay
--------------
Orwell is split into 5 episodes, each taking roughly around 40 minutes to an hour. You sit in front of a virtual computer screen representing the UI for Orwell, and you have to drag and drop highlighted bits of information from various pages (news articles/blogs/websites etc) in order to learn more about the people you're investigating. Some of these bits will be conflicting (highlighted in yellow, like addresses or opinions). You will have to listen in on conversations, read personal emails. You're basically just spying on people and using their profiles to learn more about them.

The gameplay is literally just drag and drop information onto the character it is relevant too. You don't even actually need to read anything because all the important information will be highlighted anyway. Conflicting information is important because it defines what happens to each character at the end of an episode but it's always easy to figure out which is right once you discover what both conflicting elements are (which the game will tell you anyway once you find both). You'll also have to listen to long, unskippable and un-fastforwadable phone calls for a tiny bit of information.

Design
---------
I think the game interface, while basic does look nice. It's entirely pale blue and means that the game doesn't feel aggressive or heavy. The soundtrack is forgettable, I turned it down pretty early to help me concentrate. The writing is actually pretty good but the characters and story is just unoriginal.

Problems
-------------
The biggest problem is that it's just boring. There barely is anything that constitutes real gameplay as all you're doing is dragging + dropping or waiting around for phone calls to end. As the story isn't very interesting (to me anyway) the further I got into the game the more of a chore it became. As I also said, almost everything is a straight appropriation of the older Orwellian style novels. I mean the game is called "Orwell". I seriously also hated having to wait around and listen to phone calls. It would've been better for the characters to have the call offscreen and you just get uploaded the transcript once you collect enough information (so phone calls would act like checkpoints; like the rest of the articles in the game do).

Achievements
-------------------
As the gameplay is almost non-existant, all achievements are based on what you decide to upload to Orwell. In the first episode if you upload all the peaceful things related to the first target you'll get an achievement, but if you upload how she suffers from PTSD or hates the government you'll get another. You will have to play each episode at least twice (the third episode needs to be played 3 times). Luckily there is chapter select so no achievement is missable, and the achievements are all self-contained in each chapter so choices made in chapter 1 have no impact on achievements for later chapters. I think the achievement list is pretty good.

Summary
-------------
I don't know who this game is targeted towards. If you like reading, then you've probably read 1984 OR Brave New World and as this game is basically an updated version of the book there's no need to play it. If you don't like reading then you won't like this game. I like reading, I have the BIGGEST and STRONGEST brain and i've read alot of intellectual stimuli and I still couldn't get into this game. It just does NOTHING that isn't seen in 1984 or BNW. I guess if those books are literally the best books you've ever read then you might like this but if not i'd stay away.

I've been hesitating writing a review for this one, as part of me likes the game but another part is very annoyed with it. After giving it some rest and extra thought, I have to downvote it.

The gameplay is fine, I actually quite liked that. The concept works and I would have loved a much more difficult version using this technique.

Sadly, the story is very flawed and made in such a way to get the game's "message" out. It is very biased towards why all this is a bad idea and pretty much gives no indication why and how it could actually work. And you know, that all would have been fine if done right, but everything in the story hinges on a lot of coincidences and it takes away from how an actual Orwell system could maybe properly work.

It still wouldn't, but this case does not show the actual flaws of such a system. And that is the problem of this game. It starts off by you following ONE suspect. In a true case you would have had information on everyone at the crime scene, and this is only the first big flaw why this is a bad representation of a system like this. [spoiler]And then that suspect ends up not being involved at all, but by coincidence she does happen to be in contact with the true criminal. Oh, sure, the writers eventually tried to make a link and explain it was the criminal who was responsible for the first suspect to be a the crime scene. Which ends up with the story making even less sense as there is absolutely no indication why the criminal would even want this suspect to be at the first crime scene.[/spoiler] And it just goes downhill from there, with more random stuff happening that just happens to be convenient for this poor mirror or a true spying system.

Conclusion: Good concept, but the writing keeps it from being a good game.

review_text_raw:
[h1]Product received for free on Humble Bundle GIveaway[/h1]

So I got this game for free on HB, and was eager to try it out. As I am a fan of [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dystopia]dystopian[/url] novels and games. Fictions like [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four]1984[/url] or [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brave_New_World]Brave New World[/url] are what I'd love to read.

This game is based off George Orwell's 1984(hence the game's name [i]Orwell[/i]). A government launching a surveillance system in a bid to stop "terrorists" and their "attacks". You are one of the agents that helps submitting [i]correct[/i] information to government intel. Suspects will be arrested or able to escape from arrestments based on what information you provided. Much like [url=https://store.steampowered.com/agecheck/app/475550/]Beholder[/url], you can save innocents or those you want to help by not submitting certain data to the Orwell system.

After a few minutes into the game, I decide that this game is quite worth the pennies. It allows you to experience being a "Big Brother" - watching citizens behind, logging every moves they make, and determining their ultimate fate. Although the Big Brother perspective is already popular among dystopian games. I find this one quite interesting. Unlike beholder, you don't need to go around maintaining good terms with residents. Instead you sit right in front of a surveillance system, pretty much like the real world NSA agents would do in their everyday work.

To sum up, I would recommend this game to everyone. Still thinking your privacy is REALLY SAFE online? On the fence of thinking about being spyed on? Play this game.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]About the Game[/h1]
Orwell is a game in which you have to read through articles, conversations and the likes to find bits of information to uncover a terrorist act. Depending on which information you present or withold, your superiors gain a different image of a person - which in turn can affect the outcome of the story.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
If you expect action-packed run'n'gun gameplay, this game is not for you. Instead, try to see it more as a mystery/interactive puzzle game. You read through a person's Blog and try to understand their motivation. Suddenly, you realize that two people you were investigating had a connection to each other, and thus you delve deeper into the story.

[h1]Theme / Story[/h1]
It couldn't be more relevant or timely. The game touches subjects like terrorism, state surveillance, how much information we present of ourselves or how much power the state should have. I enjoyed the perspective of "The Man" very much, as usually these dystopian futures are experienced through resistance fighters (because guns!).

[h1]Would I recommend it?[/h1]
Yes and no. First of all, if you are one of those "This isn't a game"-people, you just won't have fun with it.
Second, if you are anxious to make the "wrong" choice in a game (like me, for instance - [i]Datachunk marked[/i]), then this game might be troublesome for you.

You see, I tend to play these games like this: First, I select which outcome I want to achieve (e.g. save person X) and then act how I believe this outcome can be achieved.
However, Orwell is far better experienced (in my opinion) to just "do" and let the events unfold.

But as I said, if you are anxious about making the wrong call, you might not enjoy this game.
If you are neither scared by that nor by "this-isn't-a-game"-sayers, then you might really enjoy this game. I picked it up at a sale and enjoyed my time with it - hopefully you will too.
